text:
On Veterans Day, the House passed the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (H.R. 9237) (“TCAVA”) amid procedural controversy by voice vote, advancing a legislative package of nearly 60 bills addressing veterans’ disability compensation, healthcare, survivor benefits and Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) operations. Introduced by House Veterans’ Affairs Committee Chairman Mike Bost (R-IL), the legislation had stalled in July over disagreements surrounding proposed changes to disability ratings for sleep apnea and tinnitus.

The House-passed package incorporates several major veterans’ policy priorities, including the Major Richard Star Act, Love Lives On Act and Veterans’ ACCESS Act. It would expand benefits for certain disabled veterans and surviving spouses, establish new requirements for community care, improve disability claims processing and address VA workforce and infrastructure needs.

Among other provisions, the House-passed TCAVA would:

Allow certain combat-injured veterans to receive military retirement pay and VA disability compensation concurrently without reductions.

Expand survivor benefits by allowing certain surviving spouses to retain benefits following remarriage.

Increase Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC) payments and provide additional compensation for certain severely disabled veterans.

Codify eligibility standards for the Veterans Community Care Program (VCCP) and strengthen requirements for community care referrals, scheduling and provider oversight.

Establish a pilot grant program under the RECOVER Act to expand access to mental healthcare for veterans.

Improve appointment scheduling between VA facilities and community care providers.

Expand caregiver assistance and reauthorize the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program.

Improve disability claims processing, including tracking appeals and reviewing the use of automation.

Expand veterans’ education, apprenticeship and transition assistance benefits.

Address VA hiring, workforce management, procurement and infrastructure planning.

OVERVIEW OF KEY PROVISIONS

Disability Compensation and Concurrent Receipt (§ 101). TCAVA incorporates the Major Richard Star Act, allowing certain military retirees with combat-related disabilities to receive both military retirement pay and VA disability compensation without reductions. The provision would extend concurrent receipt to eligible Chapter 61 disability retirees, including those with fewer than 20 years of service, subject to statutory payment limits. The introduced legislation provides for these changes to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Survivor Benefits (§§ 102–104). The Love Lives On Act would allow eligible surviving spouses to retain DIC benefits following remarriage and prevent the termination of certain Survivor Benefit Plan annuities solely because a surviving spouse remarries. The legislation would also expand TRICARE eligibility for certain remarried surviving spouses whose subsequent marriages have ended. Additional provisions would increase DIC payments for eligible survivors and provide a supplemental monthly allowance of $833.33 for certain severely disabled veterans receiving aid and attendance benefits.

Claims Processing and Appeals (§§ 105–111). TCAVA would make several changes to VA disability claims processing, including prohibiting the denial of a claim solely because a veteran failed to appear for a medical examination. It would also establish additional tracking and reporting requirements for claims and appeals, direct the VA to develop a plan for using automation tools and improve procedures for claims involving military sexual trauma. These provisions could affect how the Veterans Benefits Administration processes claims and manages its appeals backlog.

RECOVER Act (§ 308). The RECOVER Act would establish a three-year pilot program providing grants to eligible nonprofit mental healthcare providers serving veterans. The grants would support expanded access to mental health treatment, including in-person and telehealth services, while helping providers improve care coordination and treatment outcomes.

Appointment Scheduling (§ 407). TCAVA would require the VA to implement an electronic scheduling process allowing VA schedulers to view and schedule appointments at VA facilities and with community care providers. The provision would also improve the transmission of referrals and authorization documents to non-VA providers, with the goal of reducing scheduling delays and improving coordination of care.

Community Care and Health Care Access (Title VI). The Veterans’ ACCESS Act provisions would codify community care eligibility standards and establish additional requirements for notifying veterans of their eligibility, considering continuity of care and providing information about wait times and drive times. The legislation would also address referral validity periods, community care contracting, provider training and oversight. These changes would have implications for veterans receiving care outside VA facilities and providers participating in the community care network.

Mental Health and Caregiver Support (Title III). TCAVA would expand support for family caregivers, extend and modify the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program and establish a pilot program providing grants to mental healthcare providers serving veterans. Additional provisions would address traumatic brain injuries, mental health research and access to specialized treatment programs.

VA Workforce and Infrastructure (Titles IV and VI). TCAVA would address VA personnel management, hiring processes, telework policies and workforce planning. It would also establish additional requirements for infrastructure planning, capital asset investments and procurement. These provisions are intended to improve the department’s administrative operations and management of its healthcare facilities.

DISAGREEMENTS OVER DISABILITY COMPENSATION

Despite the legislation’s broad scope, proposed changes to disability ratings for sleep apnea and tinnitus have been a central point of disagreement.

Section 108 would direct the VA to revise its disability rating schedule for sleep apnea and tinnitus. The proposed changes would generally reduce compensation available under certain ratings, including for veterans whose sleep apnea symptoms are treated through medical devices and veterans seeking compensation for tinnitus.

The changes are intended to help offset the costs of expanding other veterans’ benefits. However, several veterans service organizations (VSOs) have opposed the provisions, arguing that they would reduce compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities.

The Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW) and Disabled American Veterans (DAV) have cited VA estimates suggesting the changes could reduce disability compensation by approximately $57 billion over 10 years and affect up to 1.5 million veterans.

At the same time, more than 27 VSOs have expressed support for TCAVA, including The American Legion, Wounded Warrior Project, Military Officers Association of America, Elizabeth Dole Foundation, Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors and Gold Star Spouses of America.

Rep. Mark Takano (D-CA), ranking member of the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee, has also opposed the proposed reductions and is separately advancing the Major Richard Star Act (H.R. 2102). Rep. Takano successfully used a discharge petition to make the standalone legislation eligible for House floor consideration.

Although TCAVA includes concurrent receipt provisions, the Major Richard Star Act would address the issue without the broader package of proposed changes to disability ratings. The competing approaches underscore the disagreement over how Congress should finance expanded veterans’ benefits.

NEXT STEPS

Following House passage, TCAVA now heads to the Senate for consideration. Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee Chairman Jerry Moran (R-KS) previously introduced a companion bill (S. 4744) that includes many of the same veterans’ benefits and healthcare priorities. Sen. Moran has expressed support for advancing the legislation following House passage.

Separately, on Thursday, Nov. 12, the House passed the Major Richard Star Act by a vote of 392-18. The legislation would allow approximately 50,000 combat-injured veterans to receive their full military retirement pay alongside VA disability compensation without reductions.

The Senate could consider either approach, although the legislation’s prospects remain uncertain given disagreements surrounding disability compensation and the limited time remaining in the 119th Congress. Any differences between House and Senate legislation would need to be resolved before a bill could be sent to the president.

Brownstein will continue to monitor developments surrounding TCAVA and the Major Richard Star Act as Congress works to advance veterans’ legislation before the end of the year.

text:
Federal prosecutors have secured a guilty plea from a Florida resident accused of orchestrating a $42 million Medicare fraud scheme involving false claims for unneeded durable medical equipment (DME) and cancer genetic testing.

Chad Monroe, 48, of Tarpon Springs, Florida, pleaded guilty on November 13th, 2026, to one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and one count of wire fraud, says the U.S. Department of Justice.

Monroe and associates opened three DME companies that submitted over $26 million in false claims to Medicare, Medicare Advantage plans, and TRICARE for items such as knee, wrist, ankle, and back braces along with genetic testing that beneficiaries did not want or need.

He paid illegal kickbacks to telemedicine companies for doctors’ orders and received over $15 million in kickbacks through his company Health and Life Networking LLC by selling genetic testing orders to laboratories.

Monroe also directed a fraudulent PPP loan application for over $30,000 by misrepresenting ownership of one DME company.

Proceeds funded purchases including a 47-foot yacht called “The Rogue Shark” valued at over $600,000, a Cadillac Escalade, and other luxury vehicles, all of which authorities seized along with more than $1 million.

He faces up to 10 years in prison on the health care fraud conspiracy count and 30 years on the wire fraud charge.

Investigators from HHS-OIG, FBI, DCIS, and IRS-CI handled the case.

text:
A 47-foot yacht named “The Rogue Shark” and more than $1 million in cash now belong to the federal government after a Tarpon Springs man admitted to running a massive $42 million health care and pandemic loan scam.

Chad Monroe, 48, stood in federal court today and pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud. Prosecutors laid out how Monroe built a network of shell companies to bill Medicare, Medicare Advantage plans, and TRICARE for millions of dollars in medical braces and cancer genetic tests that patients never asked for and didn’t need.

The operation relied on three medical supply companies Monroe helped launch: Maksix Medical Products Inc., Orthotech Atlanta LLC, and 1st Choice Medical Supply LLC. Knowing his name on the paperwork would raise red flags, Monroe ordered his partners to lie on Medicare enrollment forms to disguise his ownership.

From there, the group billed federal health programs more than $26 million for unnecessary knee, wrist, ankle, and back braces. To make the paperwork look legitimate, Monroe paid illegal kickbacks to sham telemedicine companies in exchange for signed doctors’ orders. He ran a similar playbook with cancer genetic testing, using another company he controlled, Health and Life Networking LLC, to sell doctors’ orders to partner laboratories for more than $15 million in kickbacks.

When the pandemic hit, Monroe tapped into COVID-19 relief funds as well. Court records show he instructed a co-conspirator to submit a fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program loan application for more than $30,000, once again lying about who actually owned 1st Choice Medical Supply LLC.

The stolen money funded a high-end lifestyle. Aside from the $600,000 yacht, Monroe used the proceeds to buy a Cadillac Escalade and other luxury vehicles.

Monroe has not yet been scheduled for sentencing. He faces up to 10 years in federal prison for the health care fraud conspiracy charge and a maximum of 30 years for wire fraud. A federal judge will weigh U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other legal factors before handing down his final punishment.

Agents from the Department of Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General, the FBI’s Tampa office, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, and IRS Criminal Investigation unraveled the scheme. The case is being prosecuted by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, a unit launched on April 7 to back President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, which is chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance.

title: Connect to a registered nurse 24/7 with the Global Nurse Advice Line | Fort Hood Herald
description: Fort Hood-area service members, retirees and their families enrolled in TRICARE can get health advice and help finding appropriate care through the Global Nurse Advice Line, available 24/7 and 365
text:
Fort Hood-area service members, retirees and their families enrolled in TRICARE can get health advice and help finding appropriate care through the Global Nurse Advice Line, available 24/7 and 365 days a year.
What is the Global Nurse Advice Line?
The Global Nurse Advice Line, or GNAL, connects eligible beneficiaries worldwide with registered nurses who can assess symptoms, provide evidence-based health advice and recommend the appropriate level of care. A quick call or online chat may help patients determine whether they need urgent care, an emergency room or an appointment with their primary care provider.
The service also assists with scheduling same-day or next-day appointments when a nurse recommends one. This appointment assistance is available to beneficiaries enrolled at a military hospital or clinic. Virtual urgent care may also be available in some cases.
How can beneficiaries contact the advice line?
Beneficiaries in the United States, Guam and Puerto Rico can access the service by visiting the MHS Nurse Advice Line at
https://mhsnurseadviceline.com/home
for web chat or video chat, or by calling 800-TRICARE (874-2273) and selecting option 1.
Before contacting GNAL, beneficiaries should have their Department of Defense benefit number available. The number can be found on their military ID card.
Is the service available to beneficiaries stationed or traveling overseas?
Yes. The service is available to eligible TRICARE beneficiaries worldwide, including those stationed or traveling overseas.
Beneficiaries near an overseas military hospital or clinic can contact their local facility or visit the MHS Nurse Advice Line at
https://mhsnurseadviceline.com/home
to access online services and country-specific telephone numbers. When care is needed outside the Military Health System, GNAL can coordinate with the TRICARE overseas contractor.
What services can the advice line provide?
In addition to assessing symptoms, nurses can provide guidance for parents whose children are sick, help beneficiaries determine where to seek care and, when medically appropriate, provide an online absence excuse or sick slip. Beneficiaries should check their service-specific requirements for accepting such documentation.
The advice line can also help patients understand how to seek care when they have other health insurance. However, the rules of the other health insurance plan apply first, and any referred provider must be within that plan’s network.
Who is eligible to use the service?
The service is available to TRICARE beneficiaries worldwide, with exceptions for those enrolled in the US Family Health Plan or TRICARE Prime Demo, which have their own nurse advice lines.
Beneficiaries should keep their information current in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System, or DEERS, through milConnect to help ensure their eligibility.
How does GNAL support military health care providers?
For military health care providers, the advice line can help assess incoming patients and direct them to the appropriate level of care. This support can help organize appointment scheduling and guide patients to the services best suited to their needs.
What should beneficiaries do in an emergency?
GNAL is intended for health advice and care navigation, not emergencies. Anyone experiencing a medical emergency should call 911 in the United States or the applicable international emergency number overseas, or go to the nearest emergency room.
For more information, visit
TRICARE.mil/NAL
or watch the video, “Global Nurse Advice Line: Your Partner in Health”.

text:
The Defense Health Agency wants to address some of the challenges TRICARE beneficiaries face when seeking access to care. One initiative includes testing a referral-free healthcare option and developing tools to help patients find providers with available appointments.

Launched earlier this year, the TRICARE Prime demonstration project lets eligible TRICARE beneficiaries living in the Atlanta, Georgia, and Tampa, Florida, metro areas receive care through the CareSource Military and Veterans’ network instead of the Humana Military network.

The key feature being tested in the demonstration lets TRICARE Prime beneficiaries see network specialists without needing a referral.

“A lot of people have a lot of friction over referrals. If you enroll in this demonstration, the concept is it’s referral-free,” said Dan Gall, director of the TRICARE Health Plan at the Defense Health Agency, during Federal News Network’s 2027 Open Season Exchange.

Testing referral-free plan option

The project, which targets about 150,000 eligible beneficiaries, primarily focuses on active-duty family members, retirees and their families, and family members of activated National Guard or Reserve members. Active-duty service members, TRICARE for Life beneficiaries and people enrolled in premium-based plans are not eligible.

The program is built on care coordination. There are care coordination teams and a nurse advice line to help beneficiaries navigate their needs since there are no referrals. Eligible retirees, their family members and survivors will have their enrollment fees waived for the first 12 months.

“The whole intent is to remove that referral friction. A lot of patients feel burdened by the referral process. Those who feel that burden and want to try it out [can take part in] this demonstration project,” Gall said.

DHA kicked off the demonstration in January of this year. He said it’s too early to tell how the program is doing or how many people have enrolled. But data and feedback are beginning to come in. The agency plans to conduct a full evaluation of the program after the first demonstration period, Gall said.

Eligible individuals who want to try this program can enroll during the current TRICARE Open Season, which runs through Dec. 8. Changes made take effect Jan. 1.

“We are in Open Season. You can always switch, so don’t be too concerned if you’re a little hesitant on trying this program within those markets,” Gall said. “You can try it because, if it continues on and you like it, you’re in. So don’t worry about how it’s going to go in the future. I would recommend people take a strong look at it, take advantage of the Open Season and try it out.”

Ensuring healthcare accessibility

The pilot program is part of broader efforts to address issues that TRICARE beneficiaries have raised repeatedly.

TRICARE is one of the few health plans that has access standards. Beneficiaries can expect to get an initial specialty care appointment within 28 calendar days, and the agency is meeting its average time-to-appointment requirements, Gall said. The difficulty, however, tends to be finding a doctor and scheduling an appointment.

“We call it accessibility. It’s that patient burden to get the appointment or to find it in the time you want it,” he said. “We’re doing deep dives into that right now.”

Gall said the agency is working with its managed care support contractors to improve the accuracy of TRICARE’s provider directories, which list more than a million network providers nationwide.

“When you look at provider directory accuracy, we track that carefully, and of course, in every health plan, that’s a big issue because there’s little things that change on a monthly basis that affect that directory. But the perception is, ‘I can’t find the provider,’ ” Gall said.

Creating way to get swift beneficiary feedback

To address this issue, the agency is developing a tool Gall called a “hot button” that will let beneficiaries quickly report problems without requiring them to file a formal complaint. “You just hit that button on our site, and we get instant feedback,” he said.

But the problem goes beyond network directories being inaccurate or outdated.

“We’re trying to go deeper into whether it is an accuracy issue. When you go in the directory and call Dr. Gall, and my number is wrong, that’s an accuracy issue. But we’re also finding that they call Dr. Gall, I’m in the directory, but I have no appointment for you at all. Then they go to the next one, and then they go to the next one,” Gall said.

“That’s another thing we’re looking at: How do we take that burden off of the patient who is not necessarily getting the wrong number or wrong information in the directory, but who can’t find a provider that can get them their access when they need it. That’s accessibility. We’re looking at initiatives this year to lessen that burden on the patient with the managed care support contractors so they’re not sitting there taking time out of their day, making calls trying to find it.”

The agency is currently working with Humana Military and TriWest to make it easier for beneficiaries to find and schedule appointments.

“They’ve got proposals that we’re working through right now that we hope to finalize, get the necessary approvals and move forward to take that patient burden off our beneficiaries,” Gall said.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The House passed a major package of veterans bills Wednesday on Veterans Day — but not without confusion and controversy.

The centerpiece of the package is an effort to boost compensation for an estimated 58,000 veterans who are medically retired because of combat-related injuries. That objective has broad, bipartisan support in Congress, but lawmakers and veterans groups aren’t on the same page about how to get there.

The dilemma lawmakers are trying to resolve is this: Under current law, combat-injured retirees with less than 20 years of service give up a portion of their military retirement pay when they also receive Department of Veterans Affairs disability compensation. Lawmakers from both parties are trying to change that so that those retirees get all of their injury compensation and military retirement pay.

The change would lead to an average compensation boost of about $1,450 more per month, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

Republicans brought to the floor a bill that would help pay for the income boost for those retirees by changing how the department rates tinnitus or sleep apnea. Those changes would lower disability compensation for some future veterans, though they would not affect current veterans receiving compensation for those conditions. Democrats overwhelmingly opposed that trade-off and denounced the measure as the bill was debated.

“It does not take care of veterans. It takes from them,” Rep. Raul Ruiz, D-Calif., said of the Republican bill.

Republicans had to pull the bill from consideration earlier this year because they didn’t have the votes to pass it. This time, Democratic leaders again encouraged their members to oppose the measure because they said cutting benefits for one group of veterans to fund new benefits for another is not the answer.

The House chamber was packed and noisy as lawmakers talked among themselves following an earlier vote. As is the normal course of business, the House clerk read the title of the veterans bill and then the presiding officer, Rep. Addison McDowell, R-N.C., said the question for the House was on passage of the bill and that those in favor should say aye and those opposed should say no.

“The ayes have it,” McDowell said. “The bill is passed.”

Normally, Democrats would interject and ask for a roll call vote. But none came. And Republicans simply put the onus on Democrats, with Rep. Mike Bost, chairman of the House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs, calling Democrats “asleep at the wheel.”

“If nobody calls for the vote, it’s passed, which is a good thing,” said House Majority Leader Steve Scalise.

“If a few of them want to go voice their objections, they can go and make it clear on the House floor why they are against our veterans on Veterans Day. But I was proud to support it,” Scalise said. “I’m glad it passed.”

Rep. Mark Takano, the ranking Democratic member of the Veterans’ Affairs Committee, said there was no opportunity for the minority to ask for a recorded vote.

“The intention was to sneak this through,” Takano said. “Well, all I can say is, I think it’s a shallow, a hollow victory because it will go nowhere in the Senate.”

Cory Geisler, the national commander-in-chief at the Veterans of Foreign Wars, blasted the voice vote in a statement.

“If congressional leaders believed this proposal was worthy of passage, they should have had the courage to let every member’s position be recorded for the country to see,” Geisler said. “Playing political games with veterans’ benefits while avoiding public accountability is cowardly and dishonorable.”

Democrats have their own bill dealing with the issue that is expected to be voted on Thursday. Supporters used a discharge petition to get around Republican leadership and force a vote on the floor. But the Democratic measure does not include offsets.

Takano said that while some Republicans have voiced concerns about the price tag of his bill they also have no problem sending soldiers to war and approving the Pentagon budgets that come with it, or in passing tax breaks that primarily benefit the wealthy.

“Why then do they insist on balancing the budget on the backs of our veterans?” Takano said.

If the Democratic-led bill passes, the Senate could pick the one it favors, or neither, leaving it for a Democratic-controlled Congress to take the issue on next year.

text:
It’s that time of year again: open enrollment season for TRICARE beneficiaries.

Through Dec. 8, military service members and their families can explore health insurance plans offered by the Defense Department and sign up for 2027 coverage.

“This is the opportunity for TRICARE beneficiaries to change their plan, if that’s what they decide they want to do,” Eileen Huck, director of government relations at the National Military Family Association, said during Federal News Network’s 2027 Open Season Exchange.

Insurance takes effect Jan. 1. Here’s what to know about TRICARE coverage in the year ahead.

TRICARE plan options for 2027

The Defense Health Agency offers two main health insurance plans for troops and their families: TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select.

Both plans are heavily subsidized by the federal government. Active-duty service members and their families can enroll in Prime and Select for free, and those troops pay nothing out of pocket for covered services. Either plan is likely far less expensive than employer-sponsored or Affordable Care Act marketplace offerings.

Prime is a cheaper option that requires users to pick a primary care provider who will manage their care and refer them to specialists. Troops are automatically enrolled in Prime upon joining the military.

Family members in Prime don’t need to hit an annual deductible before their coverage kicks in or shoulder copays for in-network care. However, families are on the hook for a portion of nonemergency services from out-of-of network providers they receive without referrals.

Select lets plan holders see specialists without referrals but charges more money out of pocket. Costs also differ based on when the plan’s sponsor joined the military, whether they are an officer or enlisted and their pay grade.

Annual deductibles are lowest for single junior enlisted troops who joined before 2018 and highest for the families of midlevel and senior enlisted troops — and all officers who joined in 2018 or later. Select plans charge a copay for most services and cap out-of-pocket costs for families as well.

Additional plans are available for those stationed or living overseas or in certain parts of the United States, National Guardsmen and Reservists, retirees and military dependents ages 21 to 26.

TRICARE Young Adult plans

Huck warned military dependents in their early 20s will face TRICARE premiums just shy of $900 per month starting Jan. 1.

DHA quietly rolled out next year’s premiums for TRICARE Young Adult plans in the insurance program’s latest operations manual. Those plans are designed for military dependents ages 21 to 26 — once they’re no longer eligible to stay on a sponsor’s plan but haven’t yet aged out of TRICARE.

Young Adult Select offers a higher deductible with more flexibility to choose providers for $394 per month. Young Adult Prime, which typically has no deductible but requires specialist referrals, costs $893 each month. That’s an 8.5% increase for Select members and a 12.5% bump for Prime members over last year’s premiums.

The new rates mean enrollees will dole out about $4,700 for Select or more than $10,700 for Prime over the course of the year, not including the additional costs of the care they receive.

A relatively small insured population, combined with a high number of healthcare encounters, result in higher premium rates, a DHA spokesperson said. Nearly 1,300 young adults were enrolled in Prime as of September, compared to more than 27,600 in Select.

How to pick a TRICARE plan

The list of covered services hasn’t changed much for 2027, Huck said, so look at which plan would provide the best access to that care. She advises insurance shoppers to consider their expected annual out-of-pocket costs, location and preferred providers when comparing plans.

“Anybody can thrive on either TRICARE plan,” she said.

TRICARE allows each family member to sign up for the plan that best suits their individual needs. If someone is more comfortable with the military medical system, Prime is their best option, Huck said. They should live in a “Prime service area” near a military treatment facility (MTF) for a better chance of finding care, she added.

If a person often needs to see specialists and wants to avoid the referral process, Select could be a better fit. But Huck urges beneficiaries to check whether their doctors participate in the TRICARE network, since it reimburses providers for their services at a lower rate than most commercial health plans.

That has caused doctors to limit the number of TRICARE patients they accept or refuse TRICARE insurance altogether. Increasing reimbursement rates is perennially floated as a fix to bring more providers into the network, though at a higher cost to the federal government.

TRICARE issues to watch

The Military Health System isn’t immune to America’s shortage of healthcare providers. Thousands of MHS jobs are sitting empty, Huck said. Complicating matters further, military hiring often moves so slowly that applicants drop out for other jobs.

Competing priorities — preparing a wartime medical force and caring for communities — are also straining the workers DoD already has. DHA is shuffling some providers to facilities where they can practice a particular specialty, building experience but leaving other clinics understaffed. At the same time, DHA has encouraged people to return to military clinics so staff can learn from a wider pool of patients.

And that’s on top of typical quirks of military life, like an influx of patients trying to schedule appointments during the summer moving season and ahead of a new school year.

“There are some locations where the TRICARE network just isn’t robust enough to meet families’ needs for certain kinds of care,” Huck said. “If you combine that with an MTF that is maybe overwhelmed or can’t fully meet the needs of the community, then you can have challenges accessing care.”

She expects to see more congressional oversight of MTFs to ensure they can adequately care for patients.

At the same time, TRICARE is working to resolve problems caused by changes in the companies responsible for ensuring the insurance program’s underlying systems run smoothly. Humana Military and TriWest Healthcare Alliance took on that work in 2025 under a pair of contracts totaling $136 billion.

“We heard stories about folks’ data being lost, referrals being lost,” Huck said. “Now we are hearing issues with people incorrectly showing up that they have other health insurance, and so … their medical bills are not being paid.”

Most of those issues are being resolved, she added, allowing beneficiaries to access the care they’re entitled to.

TRICARE pharmacy options

Military family advocates are also watching TRICARE members’ access to pharmacies. The number of in-network drugstores has dropped, raising concerns that patients may have a hard time finding the medicine they need at an affordable price.

That comes as lawmakers question whether the pharmacy benefit manager Express Scripts is abusing its TRICARE contract to make more money on specialty and mail-order medications.

“If Congress thinks that an audit of Express Scripts and its operations is appropriate, I think that is something that they should accept,” Huck said. “Sunshine is the best disinfectant.”

text:
A Florida man pleaded guilty today to a $42 million fraud on Medicare involving false claims for durable medical equipment (DME) and cancer genetic testing. He also pled guilty to fraudulently obtaining a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan.

According to court documents and statements made in court, Chad Monroe, 48, of Tarpon Springs, Florida, conspired with others to submit fraudulent claims for DME — such as knee, wrist, ankle, and back braces — and cancer genetic testing that Medicare beneficiaries did not want or need. Monroe and his co-conspirators opened three DME companies, Maksix Medical Products Inc., Orthotech Atlanta, LLC, and 1st Choice Medical Supply LLC, which they used to submit over $26 million in false and fraudulent claims to Medicare, Medicare Advantage plans, and TRICARE.

Monroe directed co-conspirators to lie on Medicare enrollment documents to hide Monroe’s ownership of and role at the companies. To generate the doctors’ orders for DME and genetic testing, Monroe paid purported telemedicine companies’ illegal kickbacks. Monroe, through his company Health and Life Networking LLC, sold the doctors’ orders for genetic testing to co-conspirator laboratories, which paid him over $15 million in illegal kickbacks.

Monroe also directed a co-conspirator to submit a fraudulent PPP loan for over $30,000 in which he and his co-conspirator lied about, among other things, the ownership of 1st Choice Medical Supply LLC to qualify for the loan.

Monroe used the proceeds of the fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, including by purchasing a 47-foot yacht valued at over $600,000 called “The Rogue Shark,” a Cadillac Escalade, and other luxury vehicles. In connection with the charges, the government seized the yacht and more than $1 million.

Monroe pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and one count of wire fraud. A sentencing date has not been set. He faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison on the health care fraud conspiracy and 30 years in prison on the wire fraud charge. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Inspector General (HHS-OIG) Special Agent in Charge Isaac M. HHS-OIG, FBI, DCIS, and IRS-CI investigated the case.

Assistant Deputy Chief Catherine Wagner, Deputy Chief D. Keith Clouser, and Trial Attorney Paul J. Koob of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Health Care Fraud Section are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. text:
By MOAA Staff

The House passed the standalone Major Richard Star Act by a bipartisan vote of 392-18 on Nov. 12, one day after approving the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (TCAVA), a legislative package including several long-term MOAA priorities for veterans, caregivers, and survivors.

Both measures now move to the Senate, where lawmakers return Nov. 16 for their post-election session. The votes mark significant progress toward relief for combat-injured retirees and improvements to benefits and services for the broader military and veteran community. Senate passage remains necessary before either measure can become law.

[TAKE ACTION: Ask Your Senators to Support the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act]

A Broad Package of MOAA Priorities

The House passed TCAVA by voice vote on Veterans Day. The omnibus package brings together more than 60 pieces of legislation, most with bipartisan support. Among other improvements, the bill would provide:

Relief for combat-injured retirees who face an unfair pay offset costing them a dollar of military retired pay for every dollar of VA disability compensation they receive.

Expanded financial, educational, and career transition support for veteran caregivers via the Veteran Caregiver Reeducation, Reemployment, and Retirement (3R) Act.

An end to the remarriage penalty faced by surviving spouses who currently lose Dependency and Indemnity Compensation and other benefits should they remarry before age 55.

A range of improvements to the VA claims process; expanded support for rural and underserved veterans; mental health and suicide prevention programs; and VA modernization efforts.

Standalone Star Act Also Advances

The Nov. 12 vote on the Major Richard Star Act followed a successful discharge effort led by Rep. Mark Takano (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee. This legislation would allow chapter 61 retirees eligible for Combat-Related Special Compensation (CRSC) to receive full retirement pay alongside their VA disability compensation.

The standalone Star Act and the related provision in TCAVA differ in how they calculate payments. Some eligible retirees would receive the same amount under either approach, while others would receive more under the standalone bill.

MOAA continues to support passage of the standalone Star Act while advocating for the broader improvements for veterans, caregivers, and survivors included in TCAVA.

Senate Action Needed

With both measures through the House, the Senate now has an opportunity to advance these long-sought priorities before the 119th Congress ends. Neither House vote changes current benefits, as legislation must pass both chambers in identical form and be signed into law by the president before enactment.

MOAA urges senators to act before the end of the year to deliver meaningful relief for combat-injured retirees and to strengthen support for veterans, caregivers, and survivors.
